name: Molbog
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Thiessen, H. Arnold. 1977. The phonemic consequences of two morphophonemic rules in Molbog; Thiessen 1980; Zorc & Thiessen 1995, Molbog: introduction and wordlist
earlier_scan.note: Phonemic articles by Thiessen plausibly state stress; no open PDF located (SIL/CAD paywalled)

new_statements.quote: In simple and compound words there is no distinctive feature of stress in Molbog. Some words have primary stress on the ultimate syllable, some on the penultimate. Some are perceived as stressed at one time on the ultimate syllable, then again on the penultimate, depending on the speaker's higher level intonation. Position of stress is not the same for all words so it is not predictable. However, no pair of words that differ in meaning and that differ phonologically only with respect to the position of stress within the word. Consequently stress is not regarded as phonemic.
new_statements.citation: Thiessen, H. Arnold. 1977. The phonemic consequences of two morphophonemic rules in Molbog. Studies in Philippine Linguistics 1(2): 1-26. Manila: Linguistic Society of the Philippines & Summer Institute of Linguistics.
new_statements.locator: p. 11, section I.D 'With regard to stress' (PDF p. 15 of the ERIC microfiche ED 159 878 scan of SIPL 1(2))
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (archive.org ERIC microfiche ED 159 878, Studies in Philippine Linguistics 1(2), 299 pp.) and rendered PDF p. 15, which carries the running head 'Two Rules in Molbog 11'. Section 'D. With regard to stress.' reads exactly as quoted: 'In simple and compound words there is no distinctive feature of stress in Molbog. Some words have primary stress on the ultimate syllable, some on the penultimate. Some are perceived as stressed at one time on the ultimate syllable, then again on the penultimate, depending on the speaker's higher level intonation. Position of stress is not the same for all words so it is not predictable. However, no pair of words that differ in meaning and that differ pho…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and confined to the last two syllables: individual words are heard with primary stress on either the ultima or the penult, some words fluctuating between the two under phrase/sentence intonation; placement is not predictable by rule but never distinguishes words, so Thiessen treats stress as non-phonemic (and does not fix a default syllable). Corroborated by Zorc & Thiessen 1995: 361 ('Neither vowel length nor stress is phonemic') and, second-hand via Zorc's review, Thiessen 1981: 10 ('Word accent in... M[olbog] falls on one of the last two syllables of a word, including both suffixed and unsuffixed forms... not contrastive').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; Thiessen speaks only of 'primary stress' (acute accent in his transcriptions) and notes (p. 5) that the semivowel member i/u of a nuclear vowel cluster never receives primary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Unassimilated loanwords (e.g. re.lus 'clock', trak 'truck', mais.tru 'teacher') are placed outside the phonemic system (p. 11 sec. I.E); Muslim personal names and some place names are exceptions to his vowel rule a -> o outside the last two syllables (p. 12), which itself references a final two-syllable window. Zorc (review of Thiessen 1981) adds that accent contrasts occasionally heard in Palawanic lects are Tagalog/Bisayan superstrata varying by idiolect.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is for 'simple and compound words'; 'word' is defined (fn. 19, p. 23) as a minimum utterance that can occur in isolation, a root or reduplicated root plus affixes. Thiessen 1981 (quoted by Zorc) explicitly includes suffixed and unsuffixed forms in the final two-syllable window. Fluctuation is attributed to 'higher level intonation', i.e. partly phrase-level. Data: Bual, Ramos Island, 1975-77.
new_statements.identity_note: Thiessen's 1977 data were collected at Bual, Ramos Island (Balabac municipality, southern Palawan) in 1975-77; he treats Molbog of Balabac, Ramos and Banggi (Sabah) as one language, = Glottolog molb1237 (no dialect split in Glottolog). Zorc & Thiessen 1995 describe the same variety. Thiessen 1981 (seen only via Zorc's review) makes a joint accent statement for three Palawano dialects (Quezon, Brooke's Point, Canipaan) plus Molbog.

sources.quote: In simple and compound words there is no distinctive feature of stress in Molbog. Some words have primary stress on the ultimate syllable, some on the penultimate. Some are perceived as stressed at one time on the ultimate syllable, then again on the penultimate, depending on the speaker's higher level intonation. Position of stress is not the same for all words so it is not predictable. However, no pair of words that differ in meaning and that differ phonologically only with respect to the position of stress within the word. Consequently stress is not regarded as phonemic.
sources.locator: p. 11, section I.D 'With regard to stress' (PDF p. 15 of the ERIC microfiche ED 159 878 scan of SIPL 1(2))
sources.note: p. 11 sec. I.D 'With regard to stress': no distinctive stress; some words stressed on the ultima, some on the penult, some vary between the two depending on higher-level intonation; position not the same for all words so not predictable, but no minimal pairs, hence stress not phonemic. p. 5: semivowel i/u in nuclear clusters never receive primary stress. fn. 3 (p. 21): acute accent marks primary stress in transcriptions. fn. 19: 'word' = minimum utterance in isolation, root (+reduplication) plus affixes.

sources.citation: Zorc, R. David. [1983-84]. Review of: Thiessen, Henry Arnold. 1981. Phonological reconstruction of Proto-Palawan (Anthropological Papers 10). Manila: National Museum. Philippine Journal of Linguistics. (offprint, zorc.net item 044; already on file under cent2091, copied here)
sources.note: Second-hand: quotes Thiessen 1981 p. 10: 'Word accent in Q[uezon], B[rooke's] P[oint], C[anipaan], and M[olbog] falls on one of the last two syllables of a word, including both suffixed and unsuffixed forms... In none of the languages are words distinguished by accent alone so accent is not contrastive on this level and is not written.' Zorc finds this ambiguous (oxytone vs paroxytone dialects, or sporadic placement) and argues Proto-Palawan had lost PPH accent, contrasts now heard being Tagalog/Bisayan superstrata varying by idiolect.
